The sweep skeleton: events are the only coordinates where the answer can change, and an active set holds what the line currently crosses between them. For each event in order, update the active set and record what changed.
Tie-breaking at equal coordinates is where sweeps go wrong: with half-open intervals, an end is processed before a start at the same x, or an interval is wrongly counted as overlapping its neighbor.
The skyline problem: given buildings as left edge, right edge and height, output the outline. Events are left and right edges; the active set is a max-heap of heights, with lazy deletion.

The skyline walk produces seven key points as the maximum in the heap changes. A monotonic deque, from an earlier chapter, handles a window of fixed order, not a heap of arbitrary expiry like this one.

Three rectangles sum to thirty-four in area; their union is twenty-nine. Victor Klee posed the one-dimensional version in nineteen seventy-seven; Jon Bentley extended it to this two-dimensional sweep the same year.

syllabus.clause: Bentley–Ottmann segment intersection in O((n + k) log n)

at.step: Bentley–Ottmann reports every crossing among n segments: events are endpoints, known up front, plus crossings, discovered as the sweep proceeds. The active set is a balanced search tree ordered by height at the current sweep position.
The order of the tree is always the true vertical order at the sweep position, and two segments can only cross after becoming neighbors in it, so every crossing is found before the sweep reaches it.
If the number of crossings k grows as large as n squared, does a sweep costing n plus k, times log n, still beat an all-pairs scan costing n squared?

Scaling up: at n of fifty, two hundred and a thousand sparse segments, crossings grow to three, five and forty-eight, while the pairs a scan would test grow to twelve hundred, nineteen thousand and near half a million.

The one geometric primitive this needs is the sign of a cross product, exact on integer coordinates, deciding which side of a segment a point falls on. Shared endpoints, three segments through one point, or floating-point coordinates all break it.
